31 The diagram shows a thundercloud whose base is 500 m above the ground.
500 m
The potential difference between the base of the cloud and the ground is 200 MV. A raindrop with
a charge of 4.0 × 10–12
C is in the region between the cloud and the ground.
What is the electrical force on the raindrop?
A
1.6 × 10–6
N
B
8.0 × 10–4
N
C
1.6 × 10–3
N
D
0.40 N

hints: Notice the $500 \text{ m}$ separation and $200 \text{ MV}$ potential difference between the cloud base and ground, which form a large-scale uniform field.
Recall that uniform field strength is $E = V/d$, so first calculate $E$ in $\text{V m}^{-1}$ from $200 \times 10^6 \text{ V}$ and $500 \text{ m}$.
Then use $F = EQ$ with $Q = 4.0 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}$ to get the force in newtons and check the power of ten.
walkthrough: Treat the region between the cloud base and ground as an approximately uniform electric field of separation $d = 500 \text{ m}$ with potential difference $V = 200 \text{ MV} = 200 \times 10^6 \text{ V}$.
Field strength is $E = V/d$, so $E = (200 \times 10^6)/500 = 4.0 \times 10^5 \text{ V m}^{-1}$.
Force on a charge in a uniform field is $F = QE$, with $Q = 4.0 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}$.
Substitute: $F = (4.0 \times 10^{-12}) \times (4.0 \times 10^5) = 16 \times 10^{-7} \text{ N} = 1.6 \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$ with unit newton.

A.explanation: Gives $F = QE = 1.6 \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$ from the uniform field between cloud and ground.

B.explanation: Equals $QV = 8.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ J}$, which is work done moving the charge through $200 \text{ MV}$, not force - it omits division by $500 \text{ m}$.

C.explanation: About 1000 times too large, from an error in powers of ten when converting $200 \text{ MV}$ and dividing by $500 \text{ m}$.

D.explanation: Far too large for a $4.0 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}$ charge in a field of order $10^5 \text{ V m}^{-1}$.
